uses: Mealtime glucose control in type 1 and type 2 diabetes
Correction dosing for high glucose readings
quickTip: Onset 15 min, peak 30-90 min, duration 3-5 hr. Food must be on the tray before you inject.
administration: Subcut 0-15 min before a meal (or right after). Rotate sites within one region; clear solution, safe to mix with NPH by drawing lispro first.
mechanism: A modified human insulin that absorbs almost immediately, unlocking cells so glucose moves out of the blood and into tissue.
simplified: The fast key: opens the door as the meal arrives.
nursing: Check glucose before dosing; hold and notify if the patient is NPO or not eating.
Teach the 15-15 rule: 15 g fast carbs, recheck in 15 min for glucose under 70.
Hypoglycemia risk peaks 30-90 min after the dose; watch for sweating, tremor, confusion.
Monitor potassium, especially with IV fluids or when correcting high glucose.
Unopened vials in the fridge; in-use vials at room temp for 28 days.

uses: Mealtime coverage in type 1 and type 2 diabetes
IV infusion for DKA and HHS
quickTip: Onset 30-60 min, peak 2-4 hr, duration 5-8 hr. The only insulin that can be given IV.
administration: Subcut 30 min before meals. IV drip via pump for DKA; clear solution that needs no rolling and is drawn up first when mixed with NPH.
mechanism: Human insulin identical to what the pancreas makes; it binds insulin receptors and drives glucose and potassium into cells.
simplified: The workhorse: slower than lispro, and the only one that runs in an IV line.
nursing: During an IV drip, check glucose hourly and potassium every 2-4 hr; insulin pulls K+ into cells.
Hold and notify if glucose is under 70 or the patient cannot eat.
Give the subcut dose 30 min before food, then make sure the meal actually arrives.
Prime IV tubing with the insulin solution because insulin binds to plastic.
Peak at 2-4 hr is when to expect hypoglycemia; plan snacks accordingly.

uses: Basal insulin coverage, usually twice daily
Combined with regular or lispro for full-day control
quickTip: Onset 1-2 hr, peak 4-12 hr, duration 12-18 hr. Cloudy insulin: roll, never shake. Draw clear before cloudy.
administration: Subcut only, never IV. Roll the vial gently to resuspend; when mixing, inject air into NPH first, then draw regular (clear) before NPH (cloudy).
mechanism: Regular insulin bound to protamine so it dissolves slowly under the skin, giving a delayed and prolonged glucose-lowering effect.
simplified: The cloudy one with a peak: a morning dose peaks by afternoon, an evening dose peaks overnight.
nursing: A bedtime NPH dose can cause 2-3 AM hypoglycemia; offer a bedtime snack and check overnight glucose if symptomatic.
Uniformly cloudy is correct; discard if clumped or frosted.
Use a mixed NPH-regular syringe within 15 min; never mix NPH with glargine.
Teach patients to eat when the insulin peaks, not only when it is injected.
Never give IV or in an insulin pump.

uses: Once-daily basal insulin in type 1 and type 2 diabetes
Background coverage alongside mealtime rapid-acting insulin
quickTip: Onset 1-2 hr, no true peak, lasts about 24 hr. Never mix it with any other insulin.
administration: Subcut once daily at the same time every day. Clear solution but never IV; give in its own syringe or pen, never mixed.
mechanism: Forms tiny crystals in the acidic subcut depot that release insulin at a slow, steady rate around the clock.
simplified: The 24-hour flat line: background insulin with no spike.
nursing: Do not hold for a missed meal; basal insulin is still needed when NPO (though the provider may reduce the dose).
Mixing it with another insulin changes the pH and ruins the slow-release effect.
Warn patients it is clear like regular insulin; label it to prevent a mix-up.
Steady fasting glucose is the target; check morning readings.
Toujeo is a concentrated U-300 product; use only its own pen to avoid dosing errors.

quickTip: Hold 48 hr before and after IV contrast dye and watch for lactic acidosis; alone, it does not cause hypoglycemia.
administration: Take with meals to limit stomach upset; swallow extended-release tablets whole (the shell may appear in stool).
mechanism: Tells the liver to stop overproducing glucose and helps muscle respond to insulin, so blood sugar falls without extra insulin release.
simplified: Turns down the liver's sugar factory and makes cells listen to insulin again.
nursing: Check kidney function; not used when eGFR is under 30 mL/min.
Report muscle aches, deep rapid breathing, or unusual drowsiness: possible lactic acidosis.
Limit alcohol, which raises lactic acidosis risk.
Hold for surgery, dehydration, or any acute illness that could stress the kidneys.
Monitor B12 levels with long-term use.

quickTip: Take on an empty stomach first thing in the morning, same time daily, for life. Overdose looks like hyperthyroidism.
administration: Once daily with water 30-60 min before breakfast; separate from calcium, iron, and antacids by at least 4 hr.
mechanism: Synthetic T4 that the body converts to active T3, restoring the metabolic pace the failing thyroid could not set.
simplified: Replaces the missing thermostat hormone; too much and the body runs hot and fast.
nursing: Hold and notify for resting pulse over 100 or chest pain, especially in older cardiac patients.
TSH is rechecked 6-8 weeks after any dose change; symptom relief takes several weeks.
Do not switch brands without the provider; potency varies slightly.
Raises the effect of warfarin and lowers the effect of insulin; watch INR and glucose.
Missing doses returns fatigue, constipation, and cold intolerance.

uses: Preparation before thyroidectomy or radioactive iodine
quickTip: Report sore throat, fever, or mouth sores at once: agranulocytosis. Avoided in the first trimester; PTU is used instead.
administration: Orally at the same time each day, with or without food; divided doses at first, then usually once daily.
mechanism: Blocks the enzyme that attaches iodine to thyroglobulin, so the gland cannot build new T3 and T4.
simplified: Shuts down the thyroid's assembly line; stored hormone still runs out first, so effect takes weeks.
nursing: Baseline and periodic CBC and liver enzymes; hold and notify for fever or sore throat pending WBC count.
Full effect takes 4-8 weeks; a beta-blocker often bridges the gap for palpitations.
Teach signs of too much drug: weight gain, cold intolerance, fatigue (hypothyroidism).
Use reliable contraception; teratogenic early in pregnancy.
Avoid iodine-rich foods and OTC products that contain iodine.

uses: Autoimmune disease such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis
quickTip: Never stop abruptly; taper to prevent adrenal crisis. Expect high glucose, masked infection, and mood swings.
administration: Once daily in the morning with food to mirror natural cortisol and spare the stomach; taper any course longer than about 2 weeks.
mechanism: Mimics cortisol: it enters cells and switches off the genes that make inflammatory chemicals while quieting immune cells.
simplified: Borrowed cortisol that calms inflammation but tells the adrenals to take a nap.
nursing: Monitor glucose, BP, weight, and potassium; watch for edema and hypokalemia.
Fever may be blunted; report any low-grade temperature or wound change.
Teach stress dosing during illness or surgery and to carry a steroid alert card.
Encourage calcium, vitamin D, and weight-bearing exercise; report black stools.
No live vaccines while on high doses; long-term use can cause cataracts and thin skin.

uses: Postherpetic neuralgia and diabetic nerve pain
quickTip: Drowsiness and dizziness make falls the main danger. Taper over at least a week; stopping suddenly can trigger seizures.
administration: Orally with or without food, usually three times daily; separate from antacids by 2 hr. Doses are reduced for kidney impairment.
mechanism: Binds a subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels on nerve endings, reducing the release of excitatory neurotransmitters.
simplified: Puts a brake on overexcited nerves so they stop firing pain and seizure signals.
nursing: Fall precautions and no driving until the response is known.
Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants; respiratory depression is possible with opioids.
Monitor for new depression or suicidal thoughts, as with all anticonvulsants.
Check renal function; the drug is cleared unchanged by the kidneys.
Full pain relief may take 1-2 weeks; the dose is increased gradually.

quickTip: Therapeutic level 10-20 mcg/mL. Toxicity shows as nystagmus first, then ataxia, slurred speech, and confusion.
administration: IV only in normal saline through a filter at no more than 50 mg/min; use a large vein and never give IM. Oral doses with food; hold tube feeds 1-2 hr before and after.
mechanism: Keeps sodium channels in their inactive state longer, so neurons that fire too rapidly cannot sustain a seizure.
simplified: Slows the sodium gates so a spark cannot spread into a seizure storm.
nursing: Watch the IV site: purple discoloration and pain signal extravasation (purple glove syndrome); it is also a vesicant.
Monitor BP and ECG during IV loading; fast infusion causes hypotension and arrhythmias.
Teach meticulous oral hygiene and regular dental visits for gum overgrowth.
Reduces effectiveness of oral contraceptives and warfarin control; teratogenic.
Never stop abruptly; check levels with any change in dose, illness, or interacting drug.

quickTip: Antidote is flumazenil. Combining with opioids or alcohol can stop breathing; dependence develops, so taper rather than stop.
administration: IV slowly, no faster than 2 mg/min, with resuscitation equipment nearby; IM deep into a large muscle; oral doses at bedtime or divided through the day.
mechanism: Enhances GABA, the brain's main calming chemical, so neurons become harder to excite.
simplified: Turns up the volume on the brain's own off switch.
nursing: Monitor respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and sedation level after each IV dose.
Fall precautions; keep the bed low and call light within reach.
Abrupt withdrawal after regular use can cause rebound anxiety and seizures.
Watch for paradoxical agitation in children and older adults.
No alcohol, driving, or other sedatives; count doses as a controlled substance.

quickTip: Full effect takes 4-6 weeks. Watch for serotonin syndrome (fever, agitation, twitching) and for suicidal thoughts in patients under 25 early in treatment.
administration: Once daily, morning or evening, with food to reduce nausea; keep the same time. Liquid form must be diluted right before taking.
mechanism: Blocks the pump that pulls serotonin back into the sending neuron, leaving more serotonin in the synapse to act.
simplified: Keeps serotonin in the conversation longer instead of recycling it.
nursing: Never combine with an MAOI; allow a 14-day washout in either direction.
Avoid St. John's wort, tramadol, and triptans, which add serotonin risk.
Taper off slowly; sudden stopping causes dizziness, flu-like feelings, and irritability.
Energy may return before mood lifts; assess suicide risk at each visit.
Check sodium in older adults who become confused or weak.

quickTip: Therapeutic 0.6-1.2 mEq/L; toxic above 1.5. Early toxicity: coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhea; then ataxia and confusion. Keep salt and fluids steady.
administration: Orally with food to cut stomach upset; swallow ER tablets whole. Drink 2-3 L of fluid daily and keep salt intake consistent.
mechanism: A salt handled by the kidneys like sodium; it dampens overactive signaling inside neurons to level out mood swings.
simplified: Travels with sodium: lose salt or water and lithium climbs to toxic levels.
nursing: Draw levels 12 hr after the last dose; every few days at first, then every 1-3 months.
Avoid NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and thiazide diuretics, which push levels up.
Vomiting, diarrhea, heavy sweating, or a low-salt diet can cause toxicity; hold and report.
Monitor kidney function and thyroid tests; hypothyroidism is common long term.
Teratogenic (heart defects); confirm contraception and hold for a coarse tremor or slurred speech.

quickTip: High risk of EPS. Acute dystonia (neck or eye spasm) is treated with IM benztropine or diphenhydramine; fever plus rigidity means NMS, an emergency.
administration: Oral doses with water or food; IM lactate for agitation; decanoate is a deep IM depot every 4 weeks using Z-track. IV use requires ECG monitoring.
mechanism: Strongly blocks dopamine D2 receptors, quieting hallucinations and delusions but also the movement pathways that rely on dopamine.
simplified: Blocks dopamine everywhere: fewer voices, stiffer muscles.
nursing: Screen with the AIMS scale for tardive dyskinesia, which can be permanent.
Check ECG and electrolytes before IV use and with other QT-prolonging drugs.
Rise slowly; monitor orthostatic BP.
Sun protection and fluids; report constipation or trouble urinating.
Black box warning: not for dementia-related psychosis in older adults.

quickTip: Raises prolactin more than other atypicals (breast enlargement, milk production, missed periods) and causes weight gain and high glucose; EPS appears at higher doses.
administration: Orally once or twice daily with or without food; dissolvable tablets go on the tongue with dry hands. Long-acting IM every 2 weeks, overlapping oral doses for the first 3 weeks.
mechanism: Blocks dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, easing psychosis with somewhat less movement side effect than older drugs.
simplified: A gentler dopamine block with a serotonin twist; the trade-off is weight and prolactin.
nursing: Track weight, waist, fasting glucose, and lipids at baseline and regularly.
Ask about breast tenderness, milk, or menstrual changes.
Orthostatic precautions; dizziness is common in the first days.
Black box warning: increased death risk in older adults with dementia.
Report fever with muscle rigidity (NMS) or new involuntary movements.

uses: Parkinsonism after encephalitis or toxin exposure
quickTip: Improvement can take weeks; later, doses wear off early or switch on and off suddenly. High-protein meals compete with absorption.
administration: Orally on an empty stomach or with a light snack; keep protein-heavy meals away from doses. Do not crush extended-release forms.
mechanism: Levodopa crosses into the brain and is converted to dopamine; carbidopa stops that conversion in the body so more drug reaches the brain with less nausea.
simplified: Refills the brain's dopamine tank, with a bodyguard that keeps the fuel from spilling before it arrives.
nursing: Never stop abruptly; sudden withdrawal can cause a syndrome like NMS.
Rise slowly and use fall precautions; report involuntary jerky movements (dyskinesia).
Dark body fluids are harmless; warn the patient in advance.
Ask about new gambling, shopping, or sexual urges (impulse control changes).
Not given with nonselective MAOIs; use caution in glaucoma.

quickTip: Slows decline but does not cure. Extra acetylcholine slows the heart and stirs the gut: check pulse and watch for weight loss.
administration: Once daily at bedtime with or without food; switch to morning if vivid dreams or insomnia occur. Dissolvable tablets melt on the tongue.
mechanism: Blocks the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine, so the memory chemical lasts longer in the brain circuits that dementia damages.
simplified: Stops the cleanup crew so the little acetylcholine left keeps working.
nursing: Check heart rate before dosing; report a pulse under 60 or fainting spells.
Increased stomach acid raises ulcer risk, especially with NSAIDs; report black stools.
Weigh regularly; nausea and poor appetite can cause weight loss.
Anticholinergic drugs (diphenhydramine, oxybutynin) cancel out the benefit.
Teach caregivers to expect gradual slowing of decline, not recovery of lost memory.

uses: Seizure prevention in preeclampsia and eclampsia
Short-term preterm labor suppression and fetal neuroprotection
quickTip: Therapeutic 4-7 mEq/L. Toxicity appears in order: lost patellar reflex, RR under 12, urine under 30 mL/hr, then cardiac arrest. Antidote: calcium gluconate.
administration: IV by infusion pump: loading dose of 4-6 g over 15-30 min, then 1-2 g/hr; usually continued 24 hr after delivery. Deep IM Z-track only if no IV access.
mechanism: Competes with calcium at nerve endings and muscle, slowing nerve firing and relaxing smooth muscle, including the uterus and blood vessels.
simplified: Calcium's rival: it quiets nerves and relaxes muscles, and calcium gluconate reverses it.
nursing: Assess deep tendon reflexes, RR, urine output, and LOC every hour; hold and notify if any toxicity sign appears.
Keep calcium gluconate 1 g IV at the bedside for the entire infusion.
Continuous fetal monitoring; expect reduced variability, and watch the newborn for floppy tone and poor breathing.
Seizure precautions: dim quiet room, side rails padded, suction ready.
Draw serum magnesium as ordered and check for pulmonary edema (crackles, dyspnea).

quickTip: Give before the trigger, not after: 30 min before chemo or at the end of surgery. Watch QT prolongation and serotonin syndrome with SSRIs.
administration: Oral or dissolvable tablet 30 min before chemo (place ODT on tongue with dry hands); IV over 2-5 min, or 15 min for chemo doses; single IV dose limited to 16 mg.
mechanism: Blocks serotonin receptors on gut nerves and in the brain's vomiting center, so the nausea signal never gets delivered.
simplified: Cuts the serotonin phone line between the gut and the vomiting center.
nursing: Check ECG and correct low potassium or magnesium before use in at-risk patients.
Avoid with other QT-prolonging drugs such as haloperidol or antiarrhythmics.
Report agitation, fever, or muscle twitching in patients also on serotonergic drugs.
Assess bowel pattern; encourage fluids and fiber for constipation.
Do not give with apomorphine; profound hypotension can result.
